questions.q: What is the measure of a right angle in degrees?
questions.a: A right angle measures exactly 90°. If a student answers "less than 90°" or "more than 90°", they are confusing the definition of right angle with acute or obtuse angles, indicating a lack of recall of the exact boundary value.

questions.q: Explain why an angle measuring 100° cannot be classified as acute.
questions.a: An acute angle must be less than 90°, but 100° is greater than 90°, so it is obtuse. If a student says it's acute because "it's wide", they are misunderstanding the threshold—confusing visual width with the numeric threshold of 90°, revealing a failure to grasp that classification depends on precise degree measure, not appearance.

(i) 45° is acute (0° < 45° < 90°); (ii) 135° is obtuse (90° < 135° < 180°); (iii) 270° is reflex (180° < 270° < 360°). If a student labels 270° as obtuse, they are incorrectly applying the obtuse range (90°–180°) to angles beyond 180°, revealing a computational error in extending inequality ranges past 180°.

questions.q: Two angles are given: Angle P = 170°, Angle Q = 190°. Which statement is true? (A) Both are obtuse. (B) P is obtuse, Q is reflex. (C) Both are reflex. (D) P is acute, Q is obtuse.
questions.a: (B) P is obtuse (90° < 170° < 180°), Q is reflex (180° < 190° < 360°). If a student chooses (A), they are mistakenly applying the obtuse range to Q (190°), failing to recognize that angles ≥180° are not obtuse—this shows a failure to analyze the upper bound of obtuse angles.

questions.q: A student claims that an angle measuring 200° is acute because "it looks sharp when you draw it small". Is this correct? Justify your answer.
questions.a: No, it is incorrect. An acute angle must be less than 90°, but 200° is greater than 180°, so it is reflex. The student is confusing the physical representation (how the angle is drawn on paper) with its actual measure—this reveals a fundamental misunderstanding that angle classification depends on degree measure, not the size of the arc drawn, indicating a failure to evaluate the role of measurement vs. visual perception.

questions.q: Create an example of a real-world situation where you would need to distinguish between an obtuse and a reflex angle, and explain why the distinction matters.
questions.a: Example: Adjusting a satellite dish—if the angle from horizontal is 100° (obtuse), the dish points slightly upward but is still within the forward hemisphere; if it's 260° (reflex), it's pointing backward, which would point the dish away from the satellite. A poor answer would give an example without explaining why the classification (obtuse vs reflex) changes the outcome, revealing a lack of ability to create meaningful applications.
